Your work will define how the world transacts.Speed and craft compoundOur goal is to get faster as Stripe grows. We also revere craftsmanship and obsess over every detail. The tension between those two operating principles – speed and craft – defines how we work.Better defaults existWe don't assume the best way to do something is the way it's always been done. We rethink from first principles how financial services should work, and welcome new ideas from every corner of the company.Built for the bestWe power the world's most ambitious companies because we're obsessed with their success, rigorous about the details, creative in our approach, and always moving with urgency.We're building the economic infrastructure for AIAI is replatforming the global economy. Stripe is building infrastructure to make it possible, including real-time agent micropayments, protocols that let software transact autonomously and fraud prevention for a new generation of threats. These are just some of the challenges you'll be working on.Around 1.7% of global GDP runs on Stripe.Behind every transaction is something someone here built.Solve the problems that matter at scaleStripe is focused on improving the conditions for economic growth and prosperity. We're seeing less growth in the 21st century than we did in the 20th. In rich countries, slower growth corresponds to less innovation and more fractious politics. In poor countries, it means sustained material deprivation. In either case, we need to do better, and we want your help. We're at the centre of this, and we think the best work is still in front of us. hiring_pages.text: OpportunityCompatibilityEmerging talentOpen rolesOpen rolesCompatibilityWorking at Stripe is not for everyoneNot everyone finds success at Stripe. Those who do tend to share a few things in common.The right people don't always think they're rightSuccessful Stripes are rigorous thinkers who appreciate that things worth doing are rarely simple. We want people who are not afraid to be wrong, who can enthusiastically back proposals they initially opposed and who know how to support decisions with numbers and narrative. We operate in situations of substantial uncertainty and cannot afford either timidity or recklessness. The global financial system can seem like a mystifying domain. It isn't. It's made of people and computers, like many other systems you've worked on. Most Stripes don't come from finance, and they've thrived by bringing fresh perspectives. We want generalists who can parachute anywhere into our operations, learn a new field quickly and execute competently beyond their formal remit. We know that we can't be successful without nurturing the careers of both generalists and experts. People who thrive in high-conflict work environments often do not enjoy the experience here. We try to embrace kindness while still encouraging Stripes to take measured risks and act boldly, even in the absence of consensus.Who is Stripe for?Ambitious buildersWe're building solutions without clear precedent, solving problems with far-reaching consequences. The people here find that energising, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Adaptable problem solversAI is changing how the global economy works, how our customers work and how Stripes work. The people who thrive here adapt quickly and treat obstacles as opportunities.Rigorous thinkersWe argue from first principles, question assumptions, and don't stop at "good enough."The most successful Stripes are the people who have the intellectual horsepower, the curiosity to learn a very complicated business and the humility to get up every day and realise there's a huge amount of things they don't know.Conor McNamaraHead of EMEAWhat all Stripes have in commonWe're dedicated to our work and optimistic about the world. We believe entrepreneurship and free markets do good, and building what supports them matters. If that's you, read on.Motivated by our missionStripe is on a mission to grow the GDP of the internet.Ask yourself:​Do I see free markets and entrepreneurship as powerful forces for advancing progress?​Does enabling entrepreneurship and helping to unlock the internet economy's full potential seem like a compelling use of my time and talents?Embody our operating principles“Users first” is a cornerstone principle. Our users trust us to provide an essential service, and it's a heavy responsibility that we take very seriously.Ask yourself:​Am I motivated to move mountains to protect and support businesses that depend on Stripe?​Am I driven to overcome obstacles and take on big things to drive progress, or do I feel overwhelmed by the sheer scale and breadth of sometimes nebulous opportunities?Energised by changeThe pace of change at Stripe and in the broader economy is accelerating. You'll work outside your domain, take on problems that didn't exist a year ago and be expected to adapt as quickly as the world does.Ask yourself:​Do I see a fast-moving environment as an opportunity rather than an obstacle?​Am I comfortable taking on problems outside my domain or experience?Collaborative, multidisciplinary workBuilding programmable financial infrastructure from first principles is inherently complex. Well-crafted work indicates care for the user, and beautiful work indicates care for the world.Move with urgency and focusWe move with speed on what matters most and take the time to invest in what will make us faster tomorrow. Whereas many companies get slower until they're eventually mired in mediocrity, we aspire to become the world's fastest company.Collaborate egolesslyWe work as one team: no fiefdoms, no hoarding information, no "not my problem." We question assumptions, debate energetically and abandon ideas when better ones emerge. We're generous with credit and stingy with blame. We learn from mistakes together.Stay curiousStripe is an applied exercise in learning about how businesses tick and how the world works. Since the details and possibilities are infinite, we are always seeking to learn. We're energised by the unfamiliar, preferring the joy of discovery to the comfort of certainty.Obsess over talentIt's every Stripe's responsibility to help hire the best and to push for excellence everywhere. Managers must relentlessly uphold our high talent bar, lead their teams with clarity and context, foster development and ultimately support Stripes in accomplishing the best work of their careers.Our cultureLike all great workplaces, Stripe has its own working culture, with norms that can surprise, delight and occasionally perplex.Friday FiresideFriday Fireside is a weekly Stripe-wide forum hosted by Patrick and John. initial_questions.prompt: Describe a backend system you have owned end-to-end for at least 2 years. What were the key architectural decisions you made, how did the system evolve, and what trade-offs did you accept?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate deep ownership over a multi-year period: initial design, scaling challenges, refactoring, incident response, and measurable outcomes. Look for evidence of long-term technical leadership, not just feature delivery.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you approach technical debt in a mature backend codebase? Give a concrete example where you balanced new feature work against refactoring or platform upgrades.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect a structured approach: identifying debt, quantifying risk/impact, proposing incremental remediation, and aligning with stakeholders. Strong answers include a specific example with before/after metrics or reduced incident rate.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how you would design a TypeScript/Node.js service that handles high-throughput asynchronous work without blocking the event loop. What patterns and libraries would you use?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss worker threads, child processes, streams, backpressure, offloading CPU-bound work, connection pooling, and avoiding synchronous APIs. Mention profiling tools and monitoring event loop lag.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key differences between TypeScript's structural type system and nominal typing in languages like Java? How does this affect API design and runtime validation?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of structural typing, excess property checks, type erasure at runtime, and the need for runtime validation (e.g., zod, io-ts). Strong answers connect this to safe API boundaries and serialization.

initial_questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL query on a large table is slow. Walk through your diagnostic process, including how you would use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, indexes, and query rewriting.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, identifying seq scans, nested loops, bad estimates, missing or unused indexes, and considering partial/covering indexes, statistics, and query restructuring. Mention pg_stat_statements and autovacuum effects.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you implement and reason about transaction isolation levels in PostgreSQL for a concurrent financial operation? Discuss anomalies like lost updates and write skew.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect clear understanding of READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE, row-level locking, SELECT FOR UPDATE, advisory locks, and serialization failures. Strong answers include retry logic and idempotency.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a distributed system that must remain available during a single-region outage. What consistency model would you choose, and how would you handle data replication and conflict resolution?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss CAP/PACELC trade-offs, multi-region replication, quorum, leader election, conflict-free replicated data types or last-write-wins, and failure detection. Look for concrete choices tied to business requirements.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once delivery semantics in distributed systems. How would you achieve effectively-once processing in practice?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of idempotency keys, deduplication stores, transactional outbox, two-phase commit limitations, and message broker guarantees. Strong answers include concrete patterns and failure scenarios.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you design a REST API for a resource that also needs to emit events when it changes? Describe versioning, idempotency, and how you would keep the API and event stream consistent.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover resource modeling, HTTP semantics, versioning strategies, idempotency keys, transactional outbox or change data capture, and eventual consistency between API responses and emitted events.

initial_questions.prompt: Compare request-response REST APIs with event-driven architectures. When would you choose one over the other, and how can they coexist in the same system?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect trade-offs around coupling, latency, scalability, observability, and failure handling. Strong answers describe hybrid patterns such as command APIs that publish events, and the operational implications of each.

initial_questions.prompt: You are deploying a Node.js service on AWS. How would you design for high availability, auto-scaling, and secure networking? Mention specific AWS services and trade-offs.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss ECS/EKS/Lambda, ALB, multi-AZ RDS, VPC design, security groups, IAM roles, secrets management, and auto-scaling policies. Look for cost and operational trade-offs.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you manage infrastructure and deployments on a cloud platform? Describe your experience with infrastructure as code, CI/CD, and rollback strategies.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect tools like Terraform, CloudFormation, CDK, or Pulumi; pipelines with automated testing; blue/green or canary deployments; and rollback plans. Strong answers include monitoring and alerting integration.

initial_questions.prompt: What are the key challenges in building payment systems, such as idempotency, reconciliation, and handling partial failures? How would you design a payment processing flow?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss idempotency keys, double-entry ledgers, reconciliation jobs, retries with exponential backoff, and handling third-party gateway failures. Look for awareness of PCI compliance and audit trails.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you ensure exactly-once processing of financial transactions in a distributed system? Discuss the limitations and practical alternatives.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of idempotent consumers, deduplication tables, transactional outbox, and the impossibility of true exactly-once in distributed systems. Strong answers focus on effectively-once with compensating actions.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain Kafka's partitioning, consumer groups, and offset management. How would you design a topic for high throughput and ordered processing?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover partition key choice, ordering guarantees per partition, consumer group rebalancing, offset commit strategies, and replication. Mention trade-offs between throughput and ordering.

initial_questions.prompt: How do you handle message processing failures and retries in Kafka? Describe patterns like dead-letter queues, retry topics, and idempotent producers.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of consumer error handling, retry topics with backoff, DLQs, idempotent producers, and transactional writes. Strong answers include monitoring and alerting for stuck consumers.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe how you would deploy and operate a Node.js application on Kubernetes. What are the key considerations for health checks, resource limits, and scaling?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss liveness/readiness probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, pod disruption budgets, rolling updates, and configuration/secrets. Look for awareness of graceful shutdown and logging.

initial_questions.prompt: What are common networking and security challenges in Kubernetes, and how would you address them? Discuss service discovery, ingress, network policies, and secrets management.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, Ingress controllers, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, secrets encryption, and service mesh options. Strong answers include zero-trust and least-privilege principles.

flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles where you built and maintained backend services, scaled systems, and solved complex problems. Quantify impact: e.g., reduced latency by X%, handled Y requests per second, led migration to microservices.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript/Node.js concepts for backend interviews?
flashcards.back: Event loop, async/await, streams, error handling, performance optimization, and building scalable APIs. Be ready to discuss trade-offs between TypeScript and plain JavaScript, and how you structure large Node.js codebases.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL queries for high performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries, use connection pooling, partition large tables, and consider materialized views. Discuss transaction isolation levels and locking.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, fault tolerance, partitioning, replication, consensus (Raft/Paxos), idempotency, and handling network partitions. Discuss trade-offs between availability and consistency.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when to use each?
flashcards.back: REST is synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and simple interactions. Event-driven is asynchronous, decoupled, good for real-time processing, scalability, and complex workflows. Often used together.

flashcards.front: What AWS services have you used for backend systems?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, ECS/EKS, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, CloudWatch. Discuss how you choose between them based on scalability, cost, and operational overhead.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers?
flashcards.back: Conduct code reviews, pair programming, design docs, knowledge sharing sessions, and setting growth plans. Provide specific examples of mentees' growth and impact.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in a remote team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written communication (RFCs, design docs), regular syncs, active listening, and inclusive decision-making. Give examples of cross-team collaboration and conflict resolution.

flashcards.front: What are key challenges in payments or financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, exactly-once processing, audit trails, PCI compliance, reconciliation, handling failures and retries, and ensuring data consistency. Discuss experience with ledgers, payment gateways, or fraud detection.

flashcards.front: How does Kafka work and why use it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform with topics, partitions, producers, consumers, and consumer groups. It provides high throughput, fault tolerance, and scalability. Used for event sourcing, stream processing, and decoupling services.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration system for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Experience with pods, deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets, and autoscaling. Discuss monitoring and troubleshooting.

questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, identifying seq scans, nested loops, bad estimates, missing or unused indexes, and considering partial/covering indexes, statistics, and query restructuring. Mention pg_stat_statements and autovacuum effects.

questions.prompt: How would you implement and reason about transaction isolation levels in PostgreSQL for a concurrent financial operation? Discuss anomalies like lost updates and write skew.
questions.answer_outline: Expect clear understanding of READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE, row-level locking, SELECT FOR UPDATE, advisory locks, and serialization failures. Strong answers include retry logic and idempotency.

questions.prompt: Design a distributed system that must remain available during a single-region outage. What consistency model would you choose, and how would you handle data replication and conflict resolution?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss CAP/PACELC trade-offs, multi-region replication, quorum, leader election, conflict-free replicated data types or last-write-wins, and failure detection. Look for concrete choices tied to business requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once delivery semantics in distributed systems. How would you achieve effectively-once processing in practice?
questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of idempotency keys, deduplication stores, transactional outbox, two-phase commit limitations, and message broker guarantees. Strong answers include concrete patterns and failure scenarios.

questions.prompt: How would you design a REST API for a resource that also needs to emit events when it changes? Describe versioning, idempotency, and how you would keep the API and event stream consistent.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover resource modeling, HTTP semantics, versioning strategies, idempotency keys, transactional outbox or change data capture, and eventual consistency between API responses and emitted events.

questions.prompt: Compare request-response REST APIs with event-driven architectures. When would you choose one over the other, and how can they coexist in the same system?
questions.answer_outline: Expect trade-offs around coupling, latency, scalability, observability, and failure handling. Strong answers describe hybrid patterns such as command APIs that publish events, and the operational implications of each.

questions.prompt: You are deploying a Node.js service on AWS. How would you design for high availability, auto-scaling, and secure networking? Mention specific AWS services and trade-offs.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss ECS/EKS/Lambda, ALB, multi-AZ RDS, VPC design, security groups, IAM roles, secrets management, and auto-scaling policies. Look for cost and operational trade-offs.

questions.prompt: How do you manage infrastructure and deployments on a cloud platform? Describe your experience with infrastructure as code, CI/CD, and rollback strategies.
questions.answer_outline: Expect tools like Terraform, CloudFormation, CDK, or Pulumi; pipelines with automated testing; blue/green or canary deployments; and rollback plans. Strong answers include monitoring and alerting integration.

questions.prompt: What are the key challenges in building payment systems, such as idempotency, reconciliation, and handling partial failures? How would you design a payment processing flow?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss idempotency keys, double-entry ledgers, reconciliation jobs, retries with exponential backoff, and handling third-party gateway failures. Look for awareness of PCI compliance and audit trails.

questions.prompt: How would you ensure exactly-once processing of financial transactions in a distributed system? Discuss the limitations and practical alternatives.
questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of idempotent consumers, deduplication tables, transactional outbox, and the impossibility of true exactly-once in distributed systems. Strong answers focus on effectively-once with compensating actions.

questions.prompt: Explain Kafka's partitioning, consumer groups, and offset management. How would you design a topic for high throughput and ordered processing?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should cover partition key choice, ordering guarantees per partition, consumer group rebalancing, offset commit strategies, and replication. Mention trade-offs between throughput and ordering.

questions.prompt: How do you handle message processing failures and retries in Kafka? Describe patterns like dead-letter queues, retry topics, and idempotent producers.
questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of consumer error handling, retry topics with backoff, DLQs, idempotent producers, and transactional writes. Strong answers include monitoring and alerting for stuck consumers.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would deploy and operate a Node.js application on Kubernetes. What are the key considerations for health checks, resource limits, and scaling?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss liveness/readiness probes, resource requests/limits, HPA, pod disruption budgets, rolling updates, and configuration/secrets. Look for awareness of graceful shutdown and logging.

questions.prompt: What are common networking and security challenges in Kubernetes, and how would you address them? Discuss service discovery, ingress, network policies, and secrets management.
questions.answer_outline: Expect discussion of ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, Ingress controllers, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, secrets encryption, and service mesh options. Strong answers include zero-trust and least-privilege principles.

questions.prompt: Describe a time when you mentored an engineer who was struggling with a technical or professional challenge. What was the situation, what did you do, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: identify the engineer and the specific struggle (e.g., debugging, system design, communication). Task: your responsibility as a mentor. Action: how you assessed their needs, set goals, provided guidance, pair programming, code reviews, regular check-ins, and adjusted your approach. Result: measurable improvement, their feedback, and long-term impact on their growth and the team.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you helped a senior engineer grow into a leadership or specialized role. How did you tailor your mentoring, and what was the result?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: the engineer's career goal and context. Task: your role in their development. Action: how you identified gaps, created stretch opportunities, provided feedback, advocated for them, and involved others. Result: their promotion or new responsibilities, impact on the team, and lessons you learned about mentoring senior engineers.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a time you had to communicate a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you ensure understanding and alignment?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: the stakeholder and the concept. Task: what needed to be communicated and why. Action: how you simplified without losing accuracy, used analogies, visuals, checked for understanding, and adapted to feedback. Result: stakeholder's decision or action, and the outcome for the project.

questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had a disagreement with a colleague or another team about a technical approach. How did you handle it, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Situation: the disagreement and stakes. Task: your goal in resolving it. Action: how you listened, sought to understand their perspective, presented data or evidence, found common ground, and escalated if necessary. Result: resolution, relationship impact, and what you learned about collaboration.

questions.prompt: Stripe processes massive volumes of financial transactions. Describe a backend system you've built over the past 5+ years that handled high throughput and required strong TypeScript/Node.js and PostgreSQL skills. What architectural decisions did you make to ensure scalability and reliability, and how did PostgreSQL fit into that design?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should detail a specific project with clear metrics (e.g., requests per second, data volume). They should explain the use of TypeScript/Node.js for the backend, including any performance optimizations. For PostgreSQL, they should discuss schema design, indexing, query optimization, replication, or partitioning. Architectural decisions might include microservices, caching, load balancing, and how they ensured data consistency and fault tolerance. They should also mention how they handled distributed system challenges like network partitions or eventual consistency.

questions.prompt: Stripe's infrastructure relies heavily on event-driven systems and cloud services. Can you walk us through a system you designed that used REST APIs and event-driven patterns, and how you leveraged AWS (or similar) and possibly Kafka? What were the trade-offs and how did you ensure reliability?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a system where they implemented REST APIs for synchronous communication and event-driven patterns (e.g., using Kafka, AWS SNS/SQS, or EventBridge) for asynchronous workflows. They should explain how they used AWS services like Lambda, ECS, or RDS, and if Kafka was used, how it was integrated. Trade-offs might include latency vs. throughput, complexity vs. decoupling, and they should discuss reliability measures like idempotency, retries, dead-letter queues, and monitoring.

questions.prompt: At Stripe, collaboration and mentorship are key. Tell us about a time you mentored an engineer or led a team through a challenging project. How did you ensure effective communication and knowledge sharing?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should provide a concrete example of mentoring or leading. They should describe the situation, their actions (e.g., pair programming, code reviews, design docs, regular check-ins), and the outcome (e.g., mentee's growth, project success). They should highlight communication skills, such as adapting to different audiences, fostering open dialogue, and resolving conflicts. Collaboration with cross-functional teams (product, design, etc.) should be evident.

questions.prompt: Stripe operates in the payments domain. Do you have any experience with payments or financial systems? If so, describe a challenge you faced and how you addressed it. If not, how would you approach learning about the domain to contribute effectively?
questions.answer_outline: If experienced: candidate should discuss specific payment-related challenges (e.g., PCI compliance, idempotency, reconciliation, fraud detection) and solutions. If not: candidate should show enthusiasm for learning, mention transferable skills (e.g., building reliable systems, handling sensitive data), and propose a plan to quickly get up to speed (e.g., studying Stripe's docs, talking to domain experts).

questions.prompt: Kubernetes is a nice-to-have for this role. Have you worked with Kubernetes in production? If so, describe how you used it to deploy and manage backend services. If not, what container orchestration technologies have you used, and how would you ramp up on Kubernetes?
questions.answer_outline: If experienced: candidate should describe deployments, scaling, service discovery, ingress, config maps, secrets, and monitoring within Kubernetes. They should mention challenges like networking, storage, or security. If not: candidate should discuss experience with Docker, ECS, or similar, and demonstrate understanding of Kubernetes concepts and willingness to learn.

questions.prompt: Designing distributed systems requires careful consideration of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Can you share an example where you had to make trade-offs in a distributed system you built, especially involving REST APIs and event-driven communication?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a specific distributed system they designed. They should explain the CAP theorem trade-offs they made (e.g., choosing AP or CP), and how that impacted the use of REST APIs (synchronous) and event-driven patterns (asynchronous). They might discuss patterns like saga, CQRS, or outbox. They should also cover how they handled failures, retries, and idempotency.

questions.prompt: Stripe's backend heavily uses TypeScript/Node.js and PostgreSQL. Can you discuss a time when you had to optimize a PostgreSQL query or schema in a Node.js application? What was the impact and how did you measure it?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe a performance issue, the diagnostic process (e.g., EXPLAIN ANALYZE, slow query logs), and the optimization (e.g., indexing, query rewriting, denormalization, connection pooling). They should mention the impact (e.g., reduced latency, increased throughput) and how they measured it (e.g., monitoring tools, benchmarks). They should also touch on how Node.js interacts with PostgreSQL (e.g., using pg, TypeORM, Prisma).

questions.prompt: Stripe runs on AWS and similar cloud platforms. Describe your experience with AWS services in a backend context. Which services have you used, and how did you ensure security, scalability, and cost-efficiency?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should list AWS services they've used (e.g., EC2, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS). They should explain how they architected for scalability (e.g., auto-scaling, load balancing), security (e.g., IAM roles, VPC, encryption), and cost-efficiency (e.g., right-sizing, reserved instances, monitoring). They might also mention infrastructure as code (e.g., CloudFormation, Terraform).

questions.prompt: Stripe values strong communication and collaboration. Give an example of a time you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder or work with a cross-functional team to deliver a project. How did you ensure alignment and success?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should provide a specific example. They should describe the audience, the approach to simplifying the concept (e.g., analogies, visuals), and the outcome. For cross-functional collaboration, they should highlight how they built relationships, managed expectations, and resolved conflicts. They should demonstrate active listening and adaptability.

flashcards.front: How would you demonstrate 5+ years of backend engineering experience in an interview?
flashcards.back: Highlight a progression of roles where you built and maintained backend services, scaled systems, and solved complex problems. Quantify impact: e.g., reduced latency by X%, handled Y requests per second, led migration to microservices.

flashcards.front: What are key TypeScript/Node.js concepts for backend interviews?
flashcards.back: Event loop, async/await, streams, error handling, performance optimization, and building scalable APIs. Be ready to discuss trade-offs between TypeScript and plain JavaScript, and how you structure large Node.js codebases.

flashcards.front: How do you optimize PostgreSQL queries for high performance?
flashcards.back: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proper indexing (B-tree, GIN, etc.), avoid N+1 queries, use connection pooling, partition large tables, and consider materialized views. Discuss transaction isolation levels and locking.

flashcards.front: What are key considerations when designing distributed systems?
flashcards.back: CAP theorem, consistency models, fault tolerance, partitioning, replication, consensus (Raft/Paxos), idempotency, and handling network partitions. Discuss trade-offs between availability and consistency.

flashcards.front: How do REST APIs and event-driven systems differ, and when to use each?
flashcards.back: REST is synchronous request-response, good for CRUD and simple interactions. Event-driven is asynchronous, decoupled, good for real-time processing, scalability, and complex workflows. Often used together.

flashcards.front: What AWS services have you used for backend systems?
flashcards.back: EC2, Lambda, ECS/EKS, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, API Gateway, CloudWatch. Discuss how you choose between them based on scalability, cost, and operational overhead.

flashcards.front: How have you mentored engineers?
flashcards.back: Conduct code reviews, pair programming, design docs, knowledge sharing sessions, and setting growth plans. Provide specific examples of mentees' growth and impact.

flashcards.front: How do you ensure strong communication and collaboration in a remote team?
flashcards.back: Use clear written communication (RFCs, design docs), regular syncs, active listening, and inclusive decision-making. Give examples of cross-team collaboration and conflict resolution.

flashcards.front: What are key challenges in payments or financial systems?
flashcards.back: Idempotency, exactly-once processing, audit trails, PCI compliance, reconciliation, handling failures and retries, and ensuring data consistency. Discuss experience with ledgers, payment gateways, or fraud detection.

flashcards.front: How does Kafka work and why use it?
flashcards.back: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform with topics, partitions, producers, consumers, and consumer groups. It provides high throughput, fault tolerance, and scalability. Used for event sourcing, stream processing, and decoupling services.

flashcards.front: What is Kubernetes and how have you used it?
flashcards.back: Kubernetes is a container orchestration system for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Experience with pods, deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets, and autoscaling. Discuss monitoring and troubleshooting.

Strong SQL and relational database knowledge
Ability to work effectively with product and engineering teams

We move with startup speed, but we’ve been around for a minute. We're technical to our core and human in our approach. We're deeply serious and seriously playful, because we know that's how the best work gets done.We give a shit and get shit done. We obsess over problems, and build out loud. We build in hard mode. From the founder in the code to the engineers who move like entrepreneurs. Hack it, break it, make it better. It’s about high agency in high ambiguity. Often starting scrappy, but always shipping polished.This environment transforms people. We raise the floor, while we constantly redefine the ceiling. The bar is high and the pace is fast, but nobody climbs alone. That's how we create extraordinary products for our merchants. That’s how we make commerce better for everyone.Ready to join? Let's go. Already built something the world knows? Skip the line.Let's goSkip the lineMakecommercebetterforeveryone.What we doLife-defining work for you—and entrepreneursWe power commerce at every scale. First-time founders at the kitchen table, global brands with stores on every continent, and everyone with a dream in between. We’re the bridge between cutting-edge technology and real merchant success. One platform, built for everyone. Since 2006, we've grown to ~8,000 employees and powered over $1 trillion in sales for millions of merchants in 175 countries. But the real story isn't in the numbers - it's in dreams realized, communities transformed, industries reimagined.How did we get here, you ask? It started with one programmer who couldn't find the right tool to sell snowboards online - so he built it himself How we buildEveryone at Shopify works on product.(Yes, even the finance team.) Product thinking, combined with our reflexive use of AI, is why our people have superpowers. It’s why we build what our merchants need before they know they need it. In a world where AI can make anything, taste and craft become our differentiator.Dive deeper: Read Tobi's AI memo.Where we hireIt's not where you sit, it's where you shipThe way we work is "Digital by Design". We do our daily work wherever we work best, and drop in to one of our Port offices whenever we feel like it. Our Ports are kinda like clubhouses for Shopifolk. Whether it's Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, New York, or Bellevue, drop in whenever you're in town.We also come together when it's obvious we need to connect. That might be big link ups in big numbers like Shopify's annual Summit in Toronto, where thousands of Shopifolk connect with each other, and our mission. It also might be Hack Days at a Port where we prototype, build, and ship fast.Or maybe it's a few days IRL (what we call: Bursts) to solve gnarly problems that can only be tackled in person. Travel happens about 3x a year, starting with Startup Connections (aka in-person onboarding with your new cohort), Shopify Summit, and at least one Burst.Our culture is built on trust, not location. We hire exceptional people wherever they are, then let them cook.Who we hireThe persistently curiousShopify has a unique personality. We hire builders with the same entrepreneurial spirit as the merchants we serve. Master crafters who know what great looks like. People who keep their identities lightweight. Who ship fast, communicate clearly, and leave things better than they found them. If you're energized by new challenges and measure success by growth - not comfort, then read on.Accept our missionCommerce is a powerful expression of free speech. We use it to cast a vote with every product we buy. You need to care deeply about your work towards our mission to make commerce better for everyone not just those you agree with.Thrive on changeWe’re building products for the long-term to make Shopify a forever company, and that requires an unrelenting pace (the week, not the quarter) and an ability to thrive in an unpredictable environment. You need to be resilient to navigate ambiguity.Chase excellenceJoining our team means working with the most driven crafters who pursue mastery. But growth isn’t just an opportunity, it’s an expectation. With resources to help you, you’ll be pushing yourself out of your comfort zone.Find your QuestJob Postings? Shopify is a company of generalists, because the best ideas come from unexpected places, and those are the ideas our merchants need to win. We connect the best people to our most important work. initial_questions.prompt: You are designing a backend service for a new product. Walk me through the key architectural decisions you would make in the first month, including how you would structure the codebase, choose a database, and plan for scalability. What trade-offs would you consider?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should demonstrate 3+ years of backend experience by discussing: separation of concerns (e.g., layered architecture), database selection (SQL vs NoSQL based on requirements), API design (RESTful endpoints), scalability considerations (horizontal scaling, caching), and deployment strategies. They should mention specific technologies and justify choices with trade-offs like consistency vs availability, development speed vs performance.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a complex backend system you have built from scratch or significantly contributed to. What were the main challenges, and how did you overcome them? Focus on technical details such as data modeling, concurrency, and performance optimization.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should provide a detailed example showing depth of experience: clear problem statement, technical challenges (e.g., handling concurrent writes, optimizing queries), solutions implemented (e.g., indexing, sharding, caching), and measurable outcomes (e.g., reduced latency, increased throughput). They should demonstrate ownership and ability to make architectural decisions.

initial_questions.prompt: In Ruby, explain the difference between a Proc and a Lambda. Provide an example where using one over the other could lead to different behavior in a backend service.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain: Procs don't check arity, Lambdas do; return behavior differs (Proc returns from enclosing method, Lambda returns from itself). Example: using a Proc in a callback might cause unexpected returns, while Lambda is safer. They should relate this to backend code, such as in Rails callbacks or service objects.

initial_questions.prompt: How does Node.js handle concurrency despite being single-threaded? Discuss the event loop, and how you would avoid blocking it in a high-traffic API.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain: event loop phases, non-blocking I/O, libuv thread pool. To avoid blocking: offload CPU-intensive tasks to worker threads or child processes, use asynchronous APIs, avoid synchronous functions like fs.readFileSync. They should mention monitoring event loop lag and using clustering.

initial_questions.prompt: Design a REST API for a simple e-commerce order management system. Define the endpoints, HTTP methods, status codes, and request/response formats. How would you handle pagination and filtering?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should propose: GET /orders (list, with pagination via query params like ?page=1&limit=10), GET /orders/{id}, POST /orders, PUT/PATCH /orders/{id}, DELETE /orders/{id}. Use proper status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 500). Response should be JSON with consistent structure. Pagination: use limit/offset or cursor-based; filtering: query parameters like ?status=shipped. Discuss HATEOAS optionally.

initial_questions.prompt: What are some best practices for versioning a REST API? Compare different versioning strategies and explain how you would implement one in a production environment.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss: URI versioning (/v1/), header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json), query parameter versioning. Compare pros/cons: URI is simple but violates REST; header is cleaner but harder to test. Implementation: use routing constraints, maintain backward compatibility, deprecation policies. Mention documentation and client communication.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN. Provide a scenario where each would be appropriate in a backend application.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should define: INNER JOIN returns matching rows; LEFT JOIN returns all left rows plus matches; FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both. Scenarios: INNER for orders with customers; LEFT for customers with optional orders; FULL for merging data from two sources. They should mention NULL handling and performance implications.

initial_questions.prompt: You have a slow query on a large table. How would you diagnose and optimize it? Discuss indexing strategies, query execution plans, and potential trade-offs.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see plan, identify full table scans, missing indexes. Suggest adding indexes on WHERE/JOIN columns, composite indexes, covering indexes. Discuss trade-offs: indexes speed reads but slow writes, use of denormalization, partitioning. Mention avoiding SELECT *, using LIMIT, and caching.

initial_questions.prompt: What is the CAP theorem? How does it apply to designing a distributed database for a high-traffic application? Give an example of a system that prioritizes consistency over availability and vice versa.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should explain: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance; can't have all three. In distributed systems, partition tolerance is necessary, so trade-off between C and A. Example: CP system like HBase (consistency over availability); AP system like Cassandra (availability over consistency). Discuss how to choose based on business requirements.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe how you would implement a distributed transaction across multiple microservices. Compare two-phase commit (2PC) and saga pattern, and explain when you would use each.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: explain 2PC (prepare/commit phases, blocking, coordinator failure issues) and saga (sequence of local transactions, compensating actions). 2PC for strong consistency but low scalability; saga for eventual consistency and high availability. Discuss implementation: saga orchestration vs choreography, idempotency, and handling failures.

initial_questions.prompt: What techniques would you use to ensure a high-traffic application remains responsive under load? Discuss caching, load balancing, and database scaling.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should mention: caching (Redis, Memcached) at various layers, CDN for static assets, load balancers (e.g., Nginx, HAProxy) with horizontal scaling, database read replicas, sharding, connection pooling, asynchronous processing (queues), and auto-scaling. They should also discuss monitoring and capacity planning.

initial_questions.prompt: You are tasked with reducing the response time of a critical API endpoint that receives 10,000 requests per second. Outline your approach, including profiling, optimization, and infrastructure changes.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: profile to identify bottlenecks (APM tools, logs), optimize code (N+1 queries, inefficient algorithms), add caching (Redis), use read replicas, consider denormalization, implement rate limiting, use CDN for cacheable responses, and possibly move to a more performant language or framework. Discuss trade-offs and measurement of improvements.

initial_questions.prompt: In an e-commerce system, how would you handle inventory management to prevent overselling during high-demand sales events? Discuss database locking, optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency, and potential use of queues.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use database transactions with row-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE), optimistic concurrency (version numbers), or pessimistic locking. For high demand, use queues to serialize inventory updates, or reserve inventory with TTL. Discuss trade-offs: locking can cause contention; queues add latency but ensure consistency. Mention idempotency and compensating actions.

initial_questions.prompt: What are some common challenges in building a shopping cart service? How would you design the data model and API to handle cart persistence, merging, and checkout?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should discuss: data model (carts, cart_items, products), handling anonymous vs logged-in users, merging carts on login, persistence (database vs session), API endpoints (add/remove/update items, get cart, checkout). Consider concurrency (multiple devices), expiration, and integration with inventory and payment.

initial_questions.prompt: Explain how GraphQL differs from REST. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using GraphQL in a backend service? Provide an example of a query and its resolver.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: compare REST (multiple endpoints, over/under-fetching) vs GraphQL (single endpoint, client-specified queries). Advantages: efficient data fetching, strong typing, introspection. Disadvantages: complexity, caching challenges, potential for expensive queries. Example: query { user(id: 1) { name posts { title } } } with resolvers for user and posts.

initial_questions.prompt: How would you handle authentication and authorization in a GraphQL API? Discuss common patterns and potential pitfalls.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use JWT or session tokens in headers, implement middleware for authentication, use directives or resolver-level checks for authorization. Pitfalls: over-fetching sensitive data, N+1 queries, lack of rate limiting. Mention use of persisted queries, depth limiting, and query cost analysis.

initial_questions.prompt: What is Kubernetes and why is it useful for deploying backend services? Explain key concepts like pods, deployments, and services.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: define Kubernetes as container orchestration, benefits (scaling, self-healing, rolling updates). Explain: Pod (smallest deployable unit), Deployment (manages replicas), Service (stable network endpoint). Mention ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress. Relate to backend deployment.

initial_questions.prompt: You need to deploy a stateful backend service (e.g., a database) on Kubernetes. What considerations and Kubernetes resources would you use? Discuss StatefulSets, persistent volumes, and networking.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use StatefulSet for stable network identities and persistent storage, PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim for storage, headless Service for stable DNS. Consider data replication, backup, and scaling. Discuss challenges: managing state, upgrades, and failure recovery.

initial_questions.prompt: What is event-driven architecture? How does it differ from request-response? Give an example of a system that benefits from event-driven design.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: define EDA (components communicate via events, loosely coupled), compare to request-response (synchronous, tight coupling). Benefits: scalability, resilience, real-time processing. Example: e-commerce order processing (order placed event triggers inventory, payment, notification). Mention message brokers like Kafka, RabbitMQ.

initial_questions.prompt: Design an event-driven system for processing user activity logs. How would you ensure reliability, ordering, and exactly-once processing? Discuss message brokers and patterns.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: choose broker (Kafka for ordering and durability), design topics/partitions, use consumer groups. For reliability: acknowledge after processing, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues. For ordering: partition by key. For exactly-once: transactional producers/consumers or idempotent writes. Discuss trade-offs and monitoring.

initial_questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you faced a complex, ambiguous problem at work. How did you approach solving it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Describe the Situation and Task, including why it was complex and ambiguous. Explain the Action you took to break down the problem, gather data, and evaluate solutions. Highlight the Result, focusing on the outcome and what you learned.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to make a decision with incomplete information. How did you handle it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Outline the Situation and Task, emphasizing the missing information. Detail the Action: how you assessed risks, consulted others, and made a judgment call. Conclude with the Result and any lessons learned about decision-making under uncertainty.

initial_questions.prompt: Give an example of a time when you collaborated with a product manager to deliver a feature. What was your role and how did you ensure alignment?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Describe the Situation and Task, including the feature and your role. Explain the Action: how you communicated with the product manager, resolved any disagreements, and ensured both teams were aligned. Share the Result, such as successful delivery and impact.

initial_questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had a conflict with a member of an engineering team. How did you resolve it?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Set the Situation and Task, describing the conflict and its impact. Detail the Action: how you addressed the issue, listened to perspectives, and worked towards a resolution. Conclude with the Result and what you learned about cross-team collaboration.

initial_questions.prompt: Shopify's backend is famously built on Ruby on Rails. Walk us through your 3+ years of backend experience: which languages and frameworks have you used most, and how would your Ruby or Node.js background translate to working in a large Rails monolith?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should quantify years of backend experience, name primary languages (Ruby/Rails, Node.js, etc.), describe scale of systems owned, and show awareness that Shopify runs a large Rails codebase. Strong answers connect past framework experience to Rails conventions and show willingness to ramp up quickly.

initial_questions.prompt: Describe a REST API you designed and shipped end to end. How did you model the data in SQL, and what decisions did you make around schema design, indexing, and query performance?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Look for a concrete API with clear resources, versioning, and auth. Candidate should discuss relational modeling, normalization vs. denormalization, indexes, N+1 avoidance, and how they measured query performance. E-commerce or high-volume examples are a plus.

initial_questions.prompt: Shopify's platform handles enormous traffic spikes, especially during flash sales and BFCM. Tell us about a high-traffic distributed system you worked on. What were the failure modes, and how did you keep it reliable under load?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe system architecture (services, queues, caches, data stores), traffic volumes, and specific reliability techniques: backpressure, retries with jitter, idempotency, circuit breakers, sharding, caching layers. Look for ownership of incidents and concrete metrics (latency, QPS, error rates).

initial_questions.prompt: Describe the hardest technical problem you've solved in a backend system. How did you break it down, what trade-offs did you consider, and what was the outcome?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Strong answers follow a structured approach: problem framing, constraints, options considered, decision rationale, implementation, and measurable result. Look for evidence of debugging complex production issues and learning from trade-offs rather than just describing a feature.

initial_questions.prompt: Give an example of a project where you worked closely with product managers and other engineering teams. How did you handle competing priorities or disagreements about scope?
initial_questions.answer_outline: Candidate should show concrete collaboration: how they gathered requirements, communicated technical constraints to product, negotiated scope, and aligned multiple teams. Look for empathy, clear communication, and examples of resolving conflict constructively.

initial_questions.prompt: Shopify powers commerce for millions of merchants and increasingly exposes GraphQL APIs. Do you have any e-commerce or GraphQL experience? If so, describe it; if not, how would you get up to speed?
initial_questions.answer_outline: This is a nice-to-have, so assess genuine exposure and curiosity. E-commerce answers might cover carts, checkout, orders, inventory, or payments. GraphQL answers should mention schema design, resolvers, N+1 concerns, and client-driven queries. If lacking, look for a credible learning plan.

initial_questions.prompt: Have you worked with Kubernetes or event-driven architectures? Describe how you've deployed services or designed asynchronous workflows, and what challenges you ran into.
initial_questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Kubernetes answers might cover deployments, scaling, health checks, and observability. Event-driven answers should mention queues, pub/sub, Kafka or similar, idempotency, ordering, and eventual consistency. Reward hands-on depth but don't penalize candidates who lack it if core must-haves are strong.

questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: compare REST (multiple endpoints, over/under-fetching) vs GraphQL (single endpoint, client-specified queries). Advantages: efficient data fetching, strong typing, introspection. Disadvantages: complexity, caching challenges, potential for expensive queries. Example: query { user(id: 1) { name posts { title } } } with resolvers for user and posts.

questions.prompt: How would you handle authentication and authorization in a GraphQL API? Discuss common patterns and potential pitfalls.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use JWT or session tokens in headers, implement middleware for authentication, use directives or resolver-level checks for authorization. Pitfalls: over-fetching sensitive data, N+1 queries, lack of rate limiting. Mention use of persisted queries, depth limiting, and query cost analysis.

questions.prompt: What is Kubernetes and why is it useful for deploying backend services? Explain key concepts like pods, deployments, and services.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: define Kubernetes as container orchestration, benefits (scaling, self-healing, rolling updates). Explain: Pod (smallest deployable unit), Deployment (manages replicas), Service (stable network endpoint). Mention ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress. Relate to backend deployment.

questions.prompt: You need to deploy a stateful backend service (e.g., a database) on Kubernetes. What considerations and Kubernetes resources would you use? Discuss StatefulSets, persistent volumes, and networking.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: use StatefulSet for stable network identities and persistent storage, PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim for storage, headless Service for stable DNS. Consider data replication, backup, and scaling. Discuss challenges: managing state, upgrades, and failure recovery.

questions.prompt: What is event-driven architecture? How does it differ from request-response? Give an example of a system that benefits from event-driven design.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: define EDA (components communicate via events, loosely coupled), compare to request-response (synchronous, tight coupling). Benefits: scalability, resilience, real-time processing. Example: e-commerce order processing (order placed event triggers inventory, payment, notification). Mention message brokers like Kafka, RabbitMQ.

questions.prompt: Design an event-driven system for processing user activity logs. How would you ensure reliability, ordering, and exactly-once processing? Discuss message brokers and patterns.
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should: choose broker (Kafka for ordering and durability), design topics/partitions, use consumer groups. For reliability: acknowledge after processing, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues. For ordering: partition by key. For exactly-once: transactional producers/consumers or idempotent writes. Discuss trade-offs and monitoring.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you faced a complex, ambiguous problem at work. How did you approach solving it?
questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Describe the Situation and Task, including why it was complex and ambiguous. Explain the Action you took to break down the problem, gather data, and evaluate solutions. Highlight the Result, focusing on the outcome and what you learned.

questions.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to make a decision with incomplete information. How did you handle it?
questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Outline the Situation and Task, emphasizing the missing information. Detail the Action: how you assessed risks, consulted others, and made a judgment call. Conclude with the Result and any lessons learned about decision-making under uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a time when you collaborated with a product manager to deliver a feature. What was your role and how did you ensure alignment?
questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Describe the Situation and Task, including the feature and your role. Explain the Action: how you communicated with the product manager, resolved any disagreements, and ensured both teams were aligned. Share the Result, such as successful delivery and impact.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time when you had a conflict with a member of an engineering team. How did you resolve it?
questions.answer_outline: Use STAR: Set the Situation and Task, describing the conflict and its impact. Detail the Action: how you addressed the issue, listened to perspectives, and worked towards a resolution. Conclude with the Result and what you learned about cross-team collaboration.

questions.prompt: Shopify's backend is famously built on Ruby on Rails. Walk us through your 3+ years of backend experience: which languages and frameworks have you used most, and how would your Ruby or Node.js background translate to working in a large Rails monolith?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should quantify years of backend experience, name primary languages (Ruby/Rails, Node.js, etc.), describe scale of systems owned, and show awareness that Shopify runs a large Rails codebase. Strong answers connect past framework experience to Rails conventions and show willingness to ramp up quickly.

questions.prompt: Describe a REST API you designed and shipped end to end. How did you model the data in SQL, and what decisions did you make around schema design, indexing, and query performance?
questions.answer_outline: Look for a concrete API with clear resources, versioning, and auth. Candidate should discuss relational modeling, normalization vs. denormalization, indexes, N+1 avoidance, and how they measured query performance. E-commerce or high-volume examples are a plus.

questions.prompt: Shopify's platform handles enormous traffic spikes, especially during flash sales and BFCM. Tell us about a high-traffic distributed system you worked on. What were the failure modes, and how did you keep it reliable under load?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should describe system architecture (services, queues, caches, data stores), traffic volumes, and specific reliability techniques: backpressure, retries with jitter, idempotency, circuit breakers, sharding, caching layers. Look for ownership of incidents and concrete metrics (latency, QPS, error rates).

questions.prompt: Describe the hardest technical problem you've solved in a backend system. How did you break it down, what trade-offs did you consider, and what was the outcome?
questions.answer_outline: Strong answers follow a structured approach: problem framing, constraints, options considered, decision rationale, implementation, and measurable result. Look for evidence of debugging complex production issues and learning from trade-offs rather than just describing a feature.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a project where you worked closely with product managers and other engineering teams. How did you handle competing priorities or disagreements about scope?
questions.answer_outline: Candidate should show concrete collaboration: how they gathered requirements, communicated technical constraints to product, negotiated scope, and aligned multiple teams. Look for empathy, clear communication, and examples of resolving conflict constructively.

questions.prompt: Shopify powers commerce for millions of merchants and increasingly exposes GraphQL APIs. Do you have any e-commerce or GraphQL experience? If so, describe it; if not, how would you get up to speed?
questions.answer_outline: This is a nice-to-have, so assess genuine exposure and curiosity. E-commerce answers might cover carts, checkout, orders, inventory, or payments. GraphQL answers should mention schema design, resolvers, N+1 concerns, and client-driven queries. If lacking, look for a credible learning plan.

questions.prompt: Have you worked with Kubernetes or event-driven architectures? Describe how you've deployed services or designed asynchronous workflows, and what challenges you ran into.
questions.answer_outline: Nice-to-have. Kubernetes answers might cover deployments, scaling, health checks, and observability. Event-driven answers should mention queues, pub/sub, Kafka or similar, idempotency, ordering, and eventual consistency. Reward hands-on depth but don't penalize candidates who lack it if core must-haves are strong.
